lines.li: [us] What does a pilgrim do on a walking day?
[them] Walk from first light, pray at noon, and ask for a door at dusk.
[us] And on the other days?
[them] We keep the hostels, mend boots and copy out the road for the next walkers.
[us] What do pilgrims eat on the road?
[them] Whatever a house gives us, and we bless it whether it's much or little.
[us] Do you ever go hungry?
[them] Sometimes, and we say a hungry walker prays better, though I'm not sure it's true.
[us] Do children walk with the fellowship?
[them] Some do, and the youngest lead the old and the blind, as Brannoc's boy did.
[us] That's a lot to ask of a child.
[them] They ask for it, it's the proudest thing a young pilgrim can do.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A shrine and a hostel, and a gate that's never barred.
[us] Never?
[them] Not in my lifetime, and the hosteller would take it badly if anyone tried.
[us] How does the fellowship get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and still we'd bless their doors.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] There's peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and our walkers can use their roads again.
[them,!their:war] We pray at anyone's shrine, so nobody has much reason to quarrel with us.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} haven't been kind to us either.
[us,their:war] That's very forgiving.
[us,!their:war] I'm glad the roads are open to you.
[them,their:war] Brannoc blessed the doors that stayed shut, and so do we.
[them,!their:war] So are we, and we'll bless every door along them.
[us] What does the fellowship make of our colony?
[them,likesus] A good house to pass, and I'll say so on the road.
[them,wary] We'll bless it all the same, as we bless every house.
[them] Peace on this house, whatever else I think of it.
[us] Thank you.
[them] It's freely given.
[us] What does a sexton's day look like?
[them] Tend the grave-gardens in the morning, dig in the afternoon, ring at dusk.
[us] Is there always someone to bury?
[them] Somewhere there is, and we go where we're needed.
[us] What does the Bell eat?
[them] Simple food, eaten quietly, with a moment for the dead before we start.
[us] For the dead?
[them] For whoever we buried that day, so they're not forgotten so soon.
[us] Do the Bell's children dig too?
[them] They learn to ring before they learn to dig, the bell matters more.
[us] Aren't they afraid of the dead?
[them] We teach them there's nothing to fear from a grave that's kept properly.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A walled grave-garden, an ossuary and a bell tower, and very quiet.
[us] It sounds a little grim.
[them] It isn't, the gardens are full of flowers and people come to sit in them.
[us] How does the Bell get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and we'll bury their dead the same as ours.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] There's peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and our sextons can walk their roads again.
[them,!their:war] Quietly, everyone needs someone to bury their dead eventually.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] We've had trouble with {WAR} ourselves.
[us,their:war] Even theirs?
[us,!their:war] Your work takes you everywhere, then.
[them,their:war] Theirs too, the ground doesn't care which side anyone was on.
[them,!their:war] Everywhere there's someone unburied, and most are glad we came.
[us] What does the Bell make of our colony?
[them,likesus] You've treated us well, and we'd come if you ever needed a bell.
[them,wary] I'd want to know whether you bury your enemies.
[them] Quiet ground, and I'd like it to stay that way.
[us] We'll keep that in mind.
[them] Do, and if you need a bell-keeper, send for one.
[us] What does a clerk of the Republic do all day?
[them] Forms, mostly, and the census, and the ration cards, all in triplicate.
[us] Is that necessary?
[them] It's how we know we're still a government, and not just a few towns.
[us] What do citizens eat?
[them] Whatever's on the ration card, which this month is barley and beans.
[us] Still rationing?
[them] We never stopped, and the cards make sure everyone gets the same.
[us] How are the Republic's children raised?
[them] In school until fifteen, and every one of them can recite the old laws.
[us] All of them?
[them] The first article at least, and the brightest ones the whole constitution.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A town hall, a post office and a radio mast, with the Civic Guard in navy at the door.
[us] It sounds very orderly.
[them] It is, and the evening broadcast starts at six exactly.
[us] How does the Republic get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] The Republic is at war with {WAR}, and the broadcast says so every evening.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] There's a treaty with {PEACEWITH} now, filed and stamped.
[them,!their:war] We treat them as foreign governments, whether they think of themselves that way or not.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] We're on bad terms with {WAR} ourselves.
[us,their:war] I hope it ends soon.
[us,!their:war] That sounds very official.
[them,their:war] It will end when the treaty is signed, and not a day before.
[them,!their:war] It is, and we keep a copy of every letter we send them.
[us] What does the Republic make of our colony?
[them,likesus] A well-run settlement, and I'll say so in my report.
[them,wary] I'd want to see your census before I said anything.
[them] I've already counted your people, out of habit.
[us] I see.
[them] Everything gets written down in the end, that's how the Republic works.
[us] What does a day on the river look like?
[them] Nets out at dawn, the ferry by noon, and fish on the racks by dusk.
[us] Do you ever get a day off?
[them] When the river's in flood, and that's no holiday.
[us] What do the river folk eat?
[them] Fish, dried, smoked, salted or fresh, and fish soup when it's cold.
[us] Don't you get tired of fish?
[them] Sometimes, and then we trade fish for something else.
[us] When do your children learn the river?
[them] Before they can walk, every child is taught to swim and to tie a knot.
[us] Which knot?
[them] The one we tie on knot night, for everyone the boats pulled out of the water.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A landing with docks and fish racks, and boats tied up three deep.
[us] Does it flood?
[them] A little every spring, so we build everything on stilts.
[us] How do the river folk get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] Badly with {WAR}, our ferries won't carry them while it lasts.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] Since the peace with {PEACEWITH}, our ferries carry them again.
[them,!their:war] Easily, we ferry anyone who pays, and the price depends on the weather.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] We've had our own trouble with {WAR}.
[us,their:war] That must cost you fares.
[us,!their:war] The river doesn't take sides, I suppose.
[them,their:war] Some fares aren't worth having, and theirs is one of them.
[them,!their:war] No, and neither do the ferries, if the fare's paid.
[us] What do the river folk make of our colony?
[them,likesus] Good neighbors, the kind you'd pull out of the water.
[them,wary] I don't know you well enough yet to lend you a boat.
[them] Dry ground, and I'd want to know where your nearest water is.
[us] We'll keep that in mind.
[them] Do, and come down to the landing if you're ever passing.
[us] What does a copyist do all day?
[them] Copies, slowly, a page in the morning and a page in the afternoon.
[us] Only two pages?
[them] Two good pages, a fast copy is worse than none.
[us] What do the society's people eat?
[them] Whatever's quickest, eaten over a book, which the archivists hate.
[us] Because of the crumbs?
[them] The crumbs and the gravy, and once a whole cup of tea.
[us] How do the society's children learn?
[them] They learn to read from copies of Hesk's eleven books, as everyone has since.
[us] Only eleven books?
[them] To start with, and after that the whole archive is theirs.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] An archive, a copy hall and a bookshop, and everyone argues in all three.
[us] About what?
[them] Anything, though the night of the fire is when it gets serious.
[us] How does the society get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and the proctors guard the archive day and night.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] We've peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and their records are open to us again.
[them,!their:war] Well, we'd rather argue than fight, and most people would rather we did.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} haven't been friends to us either.
[us,their:war] I hope the archive is safe.
[us,!their:war] Arguing is a lot cheaper than fighting.
[them,their:war] Hesk burned once, and we won't let the archive burn twice.
[them,!their:war] It is, and it leaves more time for the archive.
[us] What does the society make of our colony?
[them,likesus] You'd be worth a chapter in the region's history, and I'd like to write it.
[them,wary] I'd want to read your records before I said.
[them] I'd like to know if you keep records, and if I could copy them.
[us] We'll think about it.
[them] Please do, everything kept is something saved.
[us] What does a lineman do all day?
[them] Walks the line, climbs the masts, and mends what the weather broke.
[us] In any weather?
[them] In any weather, that's what the orange oilskins are for.
[us] What does the Line eat up on the ridges?
[them] Tinned stew, heated on the mast hut's stove.
[us] Every day?
[them] Every day, and the operators say it tastes of copper.
[us] Do your children work the Line too?
[them] They start as runners between the mast huts, carrying messages.
[us] And later?
[them] Operators if they've a good ear, linemen if they've a head for heights.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A mast on the highest ground, a radio room, and houses on the slope below.
[us] Is the radio ever off?
[them] Not since the first mast went up, and we mean to keep it that way.
[us] How does the Line get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] We're at war with {WAR}, and every mast near them is on watch.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] At peace with {PEACEWITH} now, it went out on every mast the same evening.
[them,!their:war] Fine, we carry everyone's news and sell it to everyone else.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} are no friends of ours either.
[us,their:war] Stay safe up there.
[us,!their:war] The Line hears everything first.
[them,their:war] The masts are on high ground for a reason, and we can see them coming.
[them,!their:war] Nearly everything, and we always say where we heard it.
[us] What does the Line make of our colony?
[them,likesus] Good people, I heard it from the traders and I've seen it myself.
[them,wary] Can't say yet, I've heard both kinds of talk about you.
[them] Haven't heard much about you yet, which is unusual.
[us] Fair enough.
[them] I only pass on what I can name a source for, that's the Line's rule.
[us] What does a weather-reader do all day?
[them] Watch the sky, read the glass, and write down what we feel coming.
[us] Feel?
[them] The weather is the planet thinking, and a trained mind can feel it days ahead.
[us] What does the Conclave eat?
[them] Whatever keeps through a storm, so a lot of hard bread and dried fruit.
[us] Are there storms that often?
[them] On the plateau, most weeks, and we get used to eating cold.
[us] How do your children learn to read the weather?
[them] Each one is given a vial of the rain from the day they were born.
[us] What do they do with it?
[them] Learn to read it, and when they can tell what followed, they're a reader.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] Glass towers, and shelves of sealed vials going back three hundred years.
[us] Don't the towers attract lightning?
[them] They do, so we set rods on every one, and we like to watch.
[us] How does the Conclave get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and the readers have slept badly since it began.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] At peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and we've sealed a vial for the day it was made.
[them,!their:war] Well, everyone wants to know what the weather will do.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} are no friends of ours either.
[us,their:war] I hope it passes.
[us,!their:war] It sounds like calm weather for you.
[them,their:war] Everything passes, even storms that seem settled in.
[them,!their:war] For now, and we'd know before anyone if it changed.
[us] What does the Conclave make of our colony?
[them,likesus] You've treated us well, and I'd watch your sky for you if you asked.
[them,wary] I don't know yet, and I'd want to watch you for a season first.
[them] I've been watching your sky since I arrived, out of habit.
[us] Seen anything coming?
[them] Nothing worth worrying about today.
[us] What does a vault dweller do all day?
[them] Answer the roll call, then fix whatever stopped working overnight.
[us] Is it a lot?
[them] A little more every year, and none of us knows how to make new parts.
[us] What do your people eat?
[them] The old vault rations while they last, and whatever the surface camp can grow.
[us] Do you like surface food?
[them] Most of us do now, though the old ones still find fresh food strange.
[us] Were your children born below or on the surface?
[them,them:old] I was born below, but the young ones have only known the sky.
[them] The youngest were born on the surface, and they've never seen the vault sealed.
[us] Do they go below at all?
[them] For the roll call, and to learn what the old machines do while someone still knows.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A vault door in a hillside, and a surface camp that grows a little every year.
[us] Do you still live below?
[them] The old ones do, the rest of us sleep under the sky now.
[us] How does the Vault get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and we can't afford to lose any more of our gear.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] At peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and the overseer is relieved.
[them,!their:war] We remember who kept us supplied, and we try to be good to them.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} have troubled us too.
[us,their:war] I hope you don't lose any.
[us,!their:war] I'm glad things are quiet for you.
[them,their:war] Every suit that breaks is one we can't replace, so we keep well back.
[them,!their:war] So are we, quiet years are when we learn the most.
[us] What does the Vault make of our colony?
[them,likesus] You know how to make things, and that's worth more than anything we have.
[them,wary] I'd want to know you'd teach us before we traded much.
[them,their:ahead] Your tools are simpler than ours, but you can mend yours, and we can't.
[them] You've built all this yourselves, and I'd like to know how.
[us] We'd be glad to show you some time.
[them] I'll hold you to that.
[us] What does a tamer do on a day without a bout?
[them] Train, feed, groom and train again, the animal comes first.
[us] Every day?
[them] Every day, an animal that isn't worked forgets what it learned.
[us] What does the Circuit eat?
[them] We eat after the animals do, and a good many of the hatchery's spare eggs.
[us] Eggs every day?
[them] Every day, and I've stopped minding.
[us] When do your children get their first animal?
[them] When they can look after it on their own, and not a day sooner.
[us] Do they win bouts young?
[them] Some do, but most lose their first ten, and that's how they learn.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A ring for bouts in the middle, the hatchery and stables round it, and the houses last.
[us] The houses last?
[them] The animals were there first, so they get the best ground.
[us] How does the Circuit get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, and we keep the animals well away from it.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] At peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and their tamers can come to the ring again.
[them,!their:war] Well, anyone with an animal is someone to challenge, and that's friendly enough.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} have given us trouble too.
[us,their:war] I hope the animals stay safe.
[us,!their:war] A friendly bout is a good way to meet people.
[them,their:war] The animals are the first thing we'd save, whatever happens.
[them,!their:war] The best way, and losing to a stranger is the greatest honor we have.
[us] What does the Circuit make of our colony?
[them,colony:animals] I'm already wondering which of your animals would give mine a good bout.
[them,likesus] Good people, and I'd be glad to lose to one of you.
[them,!colony:animals] Not many animals here, from what I've seen, which is a pity.
[us] We'll see.
[them] Do, the ring is always open.
[us] What does a Warden do between hunts?
[them] Mend the nets, train the hounds and read the lodge's book.
[us] Read it?
[them] The empty pages, mostly, so we remember what's still loose.
[us] What do the Wardens eat on a hunt?
[them] Whatever we carry, and we carry very little so we can move fast.
[us] And at home?
[them] Venison, mostly, from the beasts that weren't the one we were after.
[us] When does a young Warden go on their first hunt?
[them] When they can keep a lantern lit through a whole night alone.
[us] That sounds hard.
[them] It's meant to be, a lantern that goes out is how people get taken.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] A lodge, the kennels and a hall with the books, and a lantern at every gate.
[us] Are the lanterns always lit?
[them] Only when something is out there that we haven't caught yet.
[us] How do the Wardens get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, which pulls good hunters off the trails.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] At peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and we can hunt their woods again.
[them,!their:war] Well, nobody turns away a hunter who comes for the beast that took their own.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} have troubled us as well.
[us,their:war] That must leave some pages open longer.
[us,!their:war] That's good for the hunting.
[them,their:war] The beasts don't wait for wars to end, and neither can we.
[them,!their:war] It is, and for the people the beasts would take.
[us] What do the Wardens make of our colony?
[them,likesus] I'd hunt beside your people, if it came to it.
[them,wary] I'd want to see how you shoot before I hunted beside you.
[them] I've been looking at your treeline, out of habit.
[us] Is that a hunter's habit?
[them] It is, and if anything comes out of it, we'll light a lantern at your gate.
[us] What does a day at the Wheel look like?
[them] Haggling by day, welding by night, and moving the whole yard once a month.
[us] When do you sleep?
[them] On the move, mostly, the carts are comfortable enough.
[us] What does the Wheel eat?
[them] Whatever's cheap at the last town, cooked in a pan that used to be something else.
[us] Like what?
[them] Mine used to be a hubcap, and it heats very evenly.
[us] How do the Wheel's children grow up?
[them] On the carts, learning to sort scrap before they can read.
[us] Do they go to school?
[them] The school moves with the town, it's the cart with the blackboard.
[us] What is {TOWN} like?
[them] Houses on wheels, workshops on runners, and next month it'll be somewhere else.
[us] Why keep moving?
[them] We left home ahead of a fire once, and nobody's ever voted to stop.
[us] How does the Wheel get on with the other peoples?
[them,their:war] {WAR} are at war with us, so the yard moves away from them every month.
[them,their:peace,!their:war] Peace with {PEACEWITH} now, and their scrap's back on the market.
[them,!their:war] Fine, everyone throws something away, and we buy it.
[us,their:war,war:ourfoe] {WAR} have troubled us too.
[us,their:war] At least you can move.
[us,!their:war] That's a good trade to be in.
[them,their:war] Wheels are good for that, we're never in one place for long.
[them,!their:war] Best trade there is, nobody ever runs out of junk.
[us] What does the Wheel make of our colony?
[them,likesus] Good people, and I'd haggle with you any day.
[them,wary] I'll tell you when I've seen your scrap pile.
[them] You stay in one place, which I'd find very strange.
[us] We'll take that as a compliment.
[them] Do, and I'll buy whatever you throw away.
